title: Credentialism and Its Discontents
paragraphs: The steadily rising educational credentials required for occupations that objectively demand no additional actual skill has prompted economists to question whether widespread credential inflation reflects genuine skill requirements or merely serves as an inefficient sorting mechanism for employers facing abundant applicant pools.

This credential inflation imposes substantial costs on prospective workers, who increasingly must complete lengthy, expensive educational programs primarily to signal baseline competence rather than to acquire skills genuinely necessary for adequate job performance.

Some employers have begun experimenting with skills-based hiring assessments that explicitly bypass traditional credential requirements, though this approach remains a distinctly minority practice given the administrative convenience credentials continue to offer overwhelmed hiring managers.

Proponents of maintaining credential requirements argue that credentials, despite their acknowledged imperfections as skill proxies, still provide meaningful information about applicant discipline, sustained effort, and baseline competence that more targeted assessments may fail to adequately capture.

Critics counter that this argument, while not entirely without merit, insufficiently justifies the enormous cumulative societal cost credential requirements impose, particularly on capable individuals from disadvantaged backgrounds who cannot easily access expensive credentialing pathways.

This unresolved tension between credentialing's genuine informational value and its substantial societal costs likely ensures continued institutional experimentation, though wholesale abandonment of established credentialing systems appears unlikely given how deeply embedded these practices remain within existing economic infrastructure.
